Bonus questions mix two or more topics from this chapter and are tagged via mixed_topics; unlock after Level 3 or serve as a standalone challenge round. Topic drill mode: filter questions by topic across all levels, order L1->L2->L3, serve in sets of ~6. Each topic has a concept card in the 'topics' array (summary, key_formulas, worked_example, common_mistakes) shown via a 'See concept' button. Topic names in 'topics' match question 'topic' tags exactly for lookup. After a failed level, link weak topics to their drill + concept card.
meta.rendering:
All mathematical expressions in question/option/explanation/hint/concept text are plain KaTeX-compatible LaTeX wrapped in \( ... \) inline delimiters (e.g. \(A \cup B\), \(2^n\), \(\{1,2,3\}\), \(\emptyset\)). Plain HTML is used only for trivial non-math emphasis in the topics[].summary field (,
, —, –) — never inside question/option/explanation/hint fields, which are pure text + \( \)-delimited LaTeX with no other markup. Render by first inserting each field's text via innerHTML/dangerouslySetInnerHTML (so the small amount of concept-card HTML displays), then calling KaTeX's renderMathInElement (auto-render extension) on the containing element so every \( ... \) span is typeset. Required includes (KaTeX 0.16.x from a CDN): , , , then call renderMathInElement(el, {delimiters: [{left: "\\(", right: "\\)", display: false}]}) after each question/topic-card render. No display-mode ($$...$$) math is used anywhere in this bank — every expression is inline.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct definition of a set?
options: Any list of numbers written together
A well-defined collection of distinct objects
A group of related numbers only
A formula that relates two variables
questions.explanation: A \(set\) is a well-defined collection of distinct objects — 'well-defined' means there is no ambiguity about whether a given object belongs to it or not.
questions.hint: Think about what makes a collection 'well-defined' rather than vague.
distractor_logic: too vague — no 'well-defined' requirement
restricts sets to only numbers, which is false
confuses a set with a relation/function

questions.question: The set \(A=\{2,4,6,8\}\) written in set-builder form is:
options: \(A=\{x : x \text{ is an odd number}, x<10\}\)
\(A=\{x : x \text{ is an even number}, x\le 8\}\)
questions.explanation: Every element of \(A\) is even and the largest is 8, so the defining rule is 'x is an even number, \(x \le 8\)'.
questions.hint: Look for the property that is true for every listed element and false for numbers not in the list.
distractor_logic: describes odd numbers, wrong parity
multiples of 4 would give {4,8,12,...}, missing 2 and 6
solving x²=8 gives no integer solutions at all

questions.question: Which of these is an example of the empty set \(\emptyset\)?
options: \(\{x : x \text{ is a natural number}, x<1\}\)
\(\{x : x \text{ is a whole number}, x<1\}\)
questions.explanation: There is no natural number less than 1 (natural numbers start at 1), so this set has no elements — it is \(\emptyset\).
questions.hint: Check whether even one element can satisfy the condition.
distractor_logic: {0} has one element (zero), so it is not empty
whole numbers start at 0, so x=0 satisfies x<1 — not empty
this is a set containing the empty set as its single element, so it has 1 element

questions.question: Two sets \(A\) and \(B\) are called equal sets if:
options: they have the same number of elements
every element of A is an element of B, and every element of B is an element of A
their power sets have the same cardinality
questions.explanation: \(A=B\) means every element of \(A\) belongs to \(B\) and every element of \(B\) belongs to \(A\) — identical elements, not just identical size.
questions.hint: Equal sets must have exactly the same elements, not just the same count.
distractor_logic: same size describes 'equivalent' sets, not 'equal' sets — a common mix-up
finiteness has nothing to do with equality of two specific sets
equal power-set size only implies equal size, not equal elements

questions.question: Which of the following sets is a finite set?
options: \(\{x : x \text{ is a day of the week}\}\)
questions.explanation: The days of the week form a set with exactly 7 elements — a finite set. Positive integers, primes, and natural numbers are all infinite.
questions.hint: Ask whether you could ever finish listing all the elements.
distractor_logic: positive integers never end
there are infinitely many primes (a classical result)
natural numbers are infinite by definition

questions.question: If \(A=\{1,2,3\}\), which symbol correctly relates the element 2 to the set \(A\)?
questions.explanation: An individual element is related to a set using \(\in\) ('belongs to'); \(\subset\) is reserved for relating one set to another set.
questions.hint: Is 2 itself a set, or is it a member of the set \(A\)?
distractor_logic: \(\subset\) is used between two sets, not between an element and a set
\(\{2\}\) is a set, and while it IS a subset it is written \(\{2\} \subset A\), not with \(\in\) here
an element can never equal the whole set

questions.question: Which pair of sets below are equivalent but NOT equal?
questions.explanation: Equivalent sets have the same number of elements without needing identical elements. \(A=\{a,b,c\}\) and \(B=\{1,2,3\}\) both have 3 elements but different members, so they are equivalent, not equal.
questions.hint: Equivalent = same size; Equal = same elements. You need same size but different elements.
distractor_logic: these sets are both equivalent AND equal (identical elements)
repeating 2 doesn't create a new element, so this is really the same 2-element set, i.e. equal
∅ has 0 elements and {0} has 1 element — not even equivalent

questions.question: A set that has exactly one element, such as \(\{7\}\), is called a:
questions.explanation: A set with exactly one element is called a singleton set. \(\{7\}\) contains only the element 7.
questions.hint: One element — a single-ton.
distractor_logic: a null set has zero elements, the opposite case
a power set is the set of all subsets, unrelated here
a universal set is context-dependent and usually large, not size 1

questions.question: \(A\) is said to be a subset of \(B\), written \(A \subset B\), when:
options: A and B have no elements in common
every element of A is also an element of B
A has fewer elements than B
B is an element of A
questions.explanation: \(A \subset B\) formally means: whenever \(x \in A\), it follows that \(x \in B\). It says nothing directly about relative sizes.
questions.hint: Subset is about membership passing through, not about counting elements.
distractor_logic: that describes disjoint sets, a different relationship entirely
a subset can even be equal in size to B (A=B is allowed for ⊂ in the non-strict sense used here)
this reverses the relationship — confusing 'subset of' with 'element of'

questions.question: Which statement about the empty set and subsets is always TRUE?
options: \(\emptyset\) is a subset of every set
\(\emptyset\) is a subset of no set
\(\emptyset\) is a subset only of finite sets
\(\emptyset\) is an element of every set
questions.explanation: By convention (vacuously true), \(\emptyset \subset A\) for every set \(A\), because there is no element in \(\emptyset\) that could fail to be in \(A\).
questions.hint: There's no element in the empty set that could ever break the subset condition.
distractor_logic: this is the exact opposite of the true rule
the rule holds for infinite sets too, not just finite ones
confuses 'subset of' with 'element of' — ∅ is not generally an element of a set

questions.question: For the interval \((2,5]\), which of the following is true?
questions.explanation: A round bracket excludes the endpoint and a square bracket includes it, so \((2,5]\) excludes 2 and includes 5.
questions.hint: Round = excluded (open), Square = included (closed).
distractor_logic: swaps which bracket means what
square brackets on both ends would give [2,5], not (2,5]
this describes the fully open interval (2,5), missing the closed right end

questions.question: Every set is a subset of itself. This means for any set \(A\):
options: \(A \subset A \text{ only if A is infinite}\)
questions.explanation: Every element of \(A\) is trivially an element of \(A\), so \(A \subset A\) holds for every set, without exception.
questions.hint: Does every element of A belong to A? Trivially, yes.
distractor_logic: states the opposite of the true rule
this holds for every set, not just the empty set
finiteness/infiniteness is irrelevant to this basic property

questions.question: A subset \(B\) of \(A\) is called a proper subset (written \(B \subsetneq A\)) when:
options: \(B\) is a subset of \(A\) but \(B \ne A\)
questions.explanation: A proper subset must be contained in \(A\) while being strictly smaller — it cannot be equal to \(A\) itself.
questions.hint: Proper subsets leave at least one element out.
distractor_logic: the empty set can be a proper subset, but B having no elements isn't the definition itself
if B=A it is a subset but NOT a proper subset
this reverses the containment direction entirely

questions.question: Which of the following correctly represents the interval notation for \(\{x \in \mathbb{R} : -3 \le x < 4\}\)?
questions.explanation: \(-3 \le x\) means \(-3\) is included (square bracket) and \(x<4\) means \(4\) is excluded (round bracket), giving \([-3,4)\).
questions.hint: Match each inequality symbol to its bracket: ≤ / ≥ → square, < / > → round.
distractor_logic: excludes -3 even though ≤ requires it to be included
includes 4 even though the strict < requires it excluded
includes both endpoints, but 4 should be excluded

questions.question: The power set \(P(A)\) of a set \(A\) is defined as:
options: the set of all elements of A raised to a power
the set of all possible subsets of A, including \(\emptyset\) and A itself
the set of all elements NOT in A
questions.explanation: \(P(A)\) collects every possible subset of \(A\) as its elements — from the empty set up to \(A\) itself.
questions.hint: 'Power set' = the set whose members are all the subsets.
distractor_logic: 'power' here has nothing to do with exponents of elements
this describes the complement, an unrelated concept
a power set is a collection of sets, not a single element

questions.question: If a set \(A\) has \(n\) elements, the number of elements in \(P(A)\) is:
questions.explanation: Each element can either be included or excluded from a subset — 2 choices per element, \(n\) elements — giving \(2^n\) total subsets.
questions.hint: Think 'in or out' for each element independently.
distractor_logic: confuses doubling the count with the correct multiplicative rule
squares the count instead of using powers of 2
factorial counts arrangements/orderings, not subset selections

questions.question: \(P(\emptyset)\), the power set of the empty set, equals:
questions.explanation: The empty set has exactly one subset — itself. So \(P(\emptyset) = \{\emptyset\}\), a singleton set containing \(\emptyset\).
questions.hint: How many subsets does a set with 0 elements have? Just one: itself.
distractor_logic: \(P(\emptyset)\) is NOT empty — it contains one element, \(\emptyset\)
0 is a number, not related to this set-theoretic construction
P(∅) has exactly 1 element, not 2

questions.question: The universal set (usually denoted U) for a given discussion is:
options: always the set of all real numbers
the set containing all objects relevant to that particular discussion
the same as the power set
questions.explanation: The universal set is context-dependent — it is simply the set that contains every object under consideration in a given problem, and can change from problem to problem.
questions.hint: Universal set = 'everything we care about right now', not a fixed universal constant.
distractor_logic: ℝ is only one possible choice of U, not the definition itself
U can be finite (e.g. all students in a class)
the power set is built FROM a set; it is a different object entirely

questions.question: Is \(\emptyset\) always an element of \(P(A)\) for any set \(A\)?
options: Yes, because the empty set is a subset of every set
No, only if A itself is empty
No, ∅ can never belong to a power set
Yes, but only when A is finite
questions.explanation: Since \(\emptyset \subset A\) for every set \(A\), and \(P(A)\) contains every subset of \(A\), \(\emptyset \in P(A)\) always — regardless of what \(A\) is.
questions.hint: Recall: \(\emptyset\) is a subset of every set, without exception.
distractor_logic: restricts the true statement incorrectly to only A=∅
contradicts the universally true subset property of ∅
finiteness is irrelevant here — the property holds for infinite A too

questions.question: If \(A\) has 4 elements, how many proper subsets does \(A\) have?
questions.explanation: \(A\) has \(2^4=16\) subsets in total; removing \(A\) itself (the only subset that is not proper here, by the common NCERT convention) leaves \(15\) proper subsets.
questions.hint: Total subsets \(2^n\), then subtract 1 for \(A\) itself.
distractor_logic: this is the total subset count \(2^4\), forgetting to exclude A itself
halves 16 incorrectly instead of subtracting 1
off-by-one error: \(16-2\) instead of \(16-1\)

questions.question: In a Venn diagram, the universal set U is conventionally represented by:
questions.explanation: By convention, the universal set is drawn as a rectangle, and all other sets under discussion are drawn as circles (or ovals) inside it.
questions.hint: The 'outer boundary' shape is different from the shape used for individual sets.
distractor_logic: circles represent the individual sets A, B, ... inside U, not U itself
a point cannot show membership regions
triangles are not the conventional shape used for U

questions.question: In a two-circle Venn diagram for sets \(A\) and \(B\) inside \(U\), the overlapping region of the two circles represents:
questions.explanation: The region common to both circles — where both circles overlap — is exactly \(A \cap B\), the elements belonging to both \(A\) and \(B\).
questions.hint: Overlap means 'in both' — that's intersection.
distractor_logic: \(A \cup B\) is the entire shaded region of both circles together, not just the overlap
\(A - B\) is the part of A's circle excluding the overlap
\(A'\) is everything outside A's circle, unrelated to the overlap

questions.question: In a Venn diagram, the region inside the rectangle \(U\) but outside both circles \(A\) and \(B\) represents:
questions.explanation: Everything inside \(U\) that is not in \(A\) and not in \(B\) is, by definition, the complement of \(A \cup B\), i.e. \((A \cup B)'\).
questions.hint: Outside both circles = not in A and not in B.
distractor_logic: \(A \cap B\) is the overlap region, the opposite location
\(A \cup B\) is the combined shaded area of both circles, not the outside
\(A - B\) is part of A's circle, still inside a circle

questions.question: If two circles representing sets \(A\) and \(B\) inside a Venn diagram do NOT touch or overlap at all, this shows that:
options: \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint sets, i.e. \(A \cap B = \emptyset\)
questions.explanation: No overlap means there is no element common to both circles, which is exactly the definition of disjoint sets: \(A \cap B = \emptyset\).
questions.hint: No shared region drawn = no shared elements.
distractor_logic: equal sets would be drawn as the exact same circle, not two separate non-overlapping ones
a subset relationship is shown by drawing one circle entirely inside the other, not separate circles
the universal set is the rectangle, never one of the inner circles

questions.question: The union of two sets \(A\) and \(B\), written \(A \cup B\), is the set of elements that belong to:
questions.explanation: \(A \cup B = \{x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}\) — an element qualifies if it is in at least one of the two sets.
questions.hint: Union collects everything from either set, without needing overlap.
distractor_logic: 'both' describes intersection \(A \cap B\), not union
this describes \(A-B\), only part of the union
this describes the complement of the union, the opposite region

questions.question: The intersection of two sets \(A\) and \(B\), written \(A \cap B\), is the set of elements that belong to:
options: exactly one of A or B
questions.explanation: \(A \cap B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}\) — an element must belong to both sets at once.
questions.hint: Intersection needs membership in BOTH sets, not just one.
distractor_logic: this describes union \(A \cup B\), a broader set
describing exactly one set (symmetric difference) is a different, more restrictive idea than intersection
this describes \(A'\), unrelated to intersection

questions.question: The set difference \(A - B\) consists of elements that are:
options: in A but not in B
in B but not in A
questions.explanation: \(A-B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \notin B\}\) — start from \(A\) and remove whatever also appears in \(B\).
questions.hint: A − B means 'A, with B's elements taken away'.
distractor_logic: this describes \(A \cap B\), not the difference
this is \(B-A\), the difference taken in the opposite order
this describes \((A \cup B)'\), outside both sets entirely

questions.question: If \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint sets, then \(A \cap B\) equals:
questions.explanation: Disjoint sets share no common elements by definition, so their intersection has no elements — \(A \cap B = \emptyset\).
questions.hint: Disjoint literally means 'no overlap' in Venn-diagram terms.
distractor_logic: A would only be the answer if \(A \subset B\), not in general for disjoint sets
same reasoning error as with A — disjointness gives ∅, not B
the intersection is empty, the exact opposite of the entire universal set

questions.question: Which property below correctly states the commutative law for union?
questions.explanation: Commutativity means order doesn't matter: \(A \cup B = B \cup A\) for any two sets.
questions.hint: Commutative laws are always about swapping the order of the same operation.
distractor_logic: equates two DIFFERENT operations (union and intersection), which are not generally equal
\(A \cup \emptyset = A\), not \(\emptyset\) — this is the identity law, stated wrongly
\(A \cup A = A\) (idempotent law), not \(\emptyset\)

questions.question: The associative law for intersection states that for sets \(A\), \(B\), \(C\):
questions.explanation: Associativity allows regrouping of the same operation applied to three sets, without changing the result — the parentheses can shift without affecting the outcome.
questions.hint: Associative = regrouping brackets for the SAME operation applied three times.
distractor_logic: this is the distributive law, mixing two different operations, not the associative law
this is the commutative law (swapping order of two sets), not associativity of three
this is the idempotent law, involving only one set, not associativity

questions.question: Which of these correctly states the distributive law of union over intersection?
questions.explanation: Distributing union over intersection works exactly like distributing multiplication over addition: \(A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)\).
questions.hint: Distribute the outer operation across each set inside the bracket, keeping the inner operation type on the right side too.
distractor_logic: drops the intersection structure entirely, just regrouping unions (associative-looking but wrong)
incorrectly turns everything into one big intersection
ignores the bracket entirely, treating it as if it were already flat

questions.question: For any set \(A\), which of these is always TRUE?
questions.explanation: The idempotent law states \(A \cup A = A\) and \(A \cap A = A\) — combining a set with itself, by either operation, just gives the set back.
questions.hint: Combining anything with itself (union or intersection) changes nothing.
distractor_logic: \(A \cup A = A\), not \(\emptyset\) — a common sign confusion with intersection with ∅
\(A \cup \emptyset = A\) (identity law for union), not \(\emptyset\)
\(A \cap \emptyset = \emptyset\) (identity/annihilator law for intersection), not \(A\)

questions.question: The complement of a set \(A\) with respect to the universal set \(U\), written \(A'\), is defined as:
questions.explanation: \(A'\) contains every element of \(U\) that is NOT in \(A\) — everything left over once \(A\) is removed from the universal set.
questions.hint: Complement = everything in U that A leaves out.
distractor_logic: this describes \(A\) itself, not its complement
\(A \cap U = A\) always (identity law), not the complement
\(A'\) equals \(\emptyset\) only in the special case \(A=U\), not in general

questions.question: For any set \(A\) within universal set \(U\), \(A \cup A'\) always equals:
questions.explanation: \(A\) and its complement together account for every element of \(U\) — nothing is left out and nothing overlaps, so \(A \cup A' = U\).
questions.hint: A and 'not A' together should cover the whole universal set.
distractor_logic: the union of A with everything outside A cannot be empty (unless U itself is empty)
\(A\) alone is only part of \(U\), missing the complement's elements
\(A'\) alone is missing A's own elements

questions.question: For any set \(A\) within universal set \(U\), \(A \cap A'\) always equals:
questions.explanation: No element can be both 'in \(A\)' and 'not in \(A\)' at the same time, so \(A\) and \(A'\) share no elements: \(A \cap A' = \emptyset\).
questions.hint: Can anything satisfy 'in A' and 'not in A' at once?
distractor_logic: the intersection is empty, the opposite of the entire universe
A and its complement overlap in NO elements, not all of A's elements
same reasoning error mirrored for the complement side

questions.question: The complement of the universal set itself, \(U'\), equals:
questions.explanation: Every element under discussion is in \(U\), so there is nothing left outside \(U\) — hence \(U' = \emptyset\).
questions.hint: What's left over once you remove everything?
distractor_logic: \(U'\) is what's OUTSIDE U, which by definition is nothing — so it can't equal U itself
this brings in a specific unrelated set A
same issue — A' is a specific set's complement, not U's

questions.question: De Morgan's law relating union and intersection complements states:
questions.explanation: De Morgan's law: \((A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'\) — 'not (A or B)' is the same as 'not A and not B'.
questions.hint: 'Not (A or B)' logically becomes 'not A AND not B' — the operation flips.
distractor_logic: flips the operation the wrong way — should become intersection of complements, not union of complements
drops the complement entirely, leaving an unrelated identity
this states the complement equals the original union, which is false in general

questions.question: For any two finite sets \(A\) and \(B\), the correct formula for \(n(A \cup B)\) is:
questions.explanation: Simply adding \(n(A)+n(B)\) double-counts the elements common to both sets, so the overlap \(n(A \cap B)\) must be subtracted once: \(n(A \cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cap B)\).
questions.hint: Adding the two counts double-counts the shared elements — remove that double-count once.
distractor_logic: forgets to remove the double-counted overlap entirely
adds the overlap instead of subtracting it, over-correcting in the wrong direction
multiplying counts has no set-theoretic meaning here

questions.question: If \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint finite sets, then \(n(A \cup B)\) equals:
questions.explanation: For disjoint sets \(n(A \cap B)=0\), so the general formula \(n(A)+n(B)-n(A\cap B)\) simplifies to just \(n(A)+n(B)\).
questions.hint: With no overlap, there's nothing to subtract.
distractor_logic: this is the general (non-disjoint) formula; here \(n(A\cap B)=0\) so it reduces to simple addition
subtraction has no basis here — both sets contribute fully
taking the maximum ignores the smaller set's elements entirely

questions.question: For three finite sets \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), the inclusion–exclusion formula for \(n(A \cup B \cup C)\) requires subtracting:
options: only the sum of the three pairwise intersections
the three pairwise intersections, then adding back the triple intersection
nothing needs to be subtracted for three sets
questions.explanation: \(n(A\cup B\cup C) = n(A)+n(B)+n(C) - n(A\cap B)-n(B\cap C)-n(A\cap C) + n(A\cap B\cap C)\): the pairwise overlaps are subtracted (each removed the double count), then the triple overlap — subtracted three times in the process — is added back once.
questions.hint: Every pairwise overlap gets subtracted; the triple overlap needs one correction to add back.
distractor_logic: stops short — omits the crucial 'add back the triple intersection' correction, undercounting
ignores the pairwise overlaps completely
assumes no double counting occurs with three sets, which is generally false

questions.question: The roster form of \(\{x : x \in \mathbb{N}, x^2 < 25\}\) is:
questions.explanation: We need natural numbers whose square is less than 25, i.e. \(x<5\) and \(x \ge 1\), giving \(x \in \{1,2,3,4\}\) (checked: \(4^2=16<25\) but \(5^2=25\) is NOT less than 25, so 5 is excluded).
questions.hint: Test each candidate: does its square stay strictly below 25?
distractor_logic: includes 5, but \(5^2=25\) is not < 25 (boundary error)
0 is not a natural number under the standard NCERT convention (N starts at 1)
stops one short — 4 also satisfies the condition and was left out

questions.question: The roster form of \(\{x : x \in \mathbb{Z}, -2 < x < 3\}\) is:
questions.explanation: Strict inequalities exclude both endpoints, so integers strictly between \(-2\) and \(3\) are \(\{-1,0,1,2\}\).
questions.hint: Strict < and > exclude the endpoints themselves — list only what's strictly between.
distractor_logic: wrongly includes both endpoints -2 and 3
includes 3, which fails the strict inequality x<3
includes -2, which fails the strict inequality -2<x

questions.question: If \(A\) is the set of distinct letters in the word 'MATHEMATICS', then \(n(A)\) equals:
questions.explanation: M-A-T-H-E-M-A-T-I-C-S has 11 letters in total, but repeats: M, A, and T each appear twice. The distinct letters are M, A, T, H, E, I, C, S — exactly 8 of them.
questions.hint: Cross out repeated letters and count only the distinct ones.
distractor_logic: counts every letter including repeats, rather than distinct ones
over-corrects the repeat removal by one
under-counts by missing one of the 8 distinct letters

questions.question: The set-builder form of \(\{5,10,15,20,25\}\) is:
questions.explanation: Each element is 5 times a natural number from 1 to 5: \(5(1)=5\), \(5(2)=10\), ..., \(5(5)=25\) — exactly bounding the range needed.
questions.hint: Find the rule AND the bound that stops exactly at 25, not beyond.
distractor_logic: true but unbounded — this describes an infinite set of ALL multiples of 5, not just these 5
stops at n=4, giving only {5,10,15,20}, missing 25
divisibility by 25 would only give {25}, far too restrictive

questions.question: Given \(A=\{1,2,3\}\), \(B=\{3,2,1,2\}\), and \(C=\{1,1,2,3\}\), which statement is correct?
options: \(A \ne B\) because B lists an element twice
None of A, B, C are equal
questions.explanation: A set is determined only by which elements it contains, not how many times each is listed or in what order. \(B\) and \(C\) both reduce to \(\{1,2,3\}\) once repeats are ignored, so \(A=B=C\).
questions.hint: Cross out duplicate entries in the listing — a set never 'remembers' repeats.
distractor_logic: singles out C incorrectly — C also reduces to {1,2,3}
repeating an element does NOT change the set — this is a common misconception
misses that all three describe exactly the same 3-element set

questions.question: How many subsets does the set \(A=\{1,2,3\}\) have in total?
questions.hint: Use \(2^n\) with \(n=3\), and don't forget to actually list them out to double-check.
distractor_logic: forgets to count the empty set, undercounting by 1 (and also just arithmetically wrong for 2^3)
off by one above the correct total
overshoots — there is no ninth subset

questions.question: Given \(A=\{2,4,6\}\) and \(B=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\), which statement is TRUE?
questions.explanation: Every element of \(A\) (2, 4, 6) is present in \(B\), so \(A \subset B\) holds. \(B\) has elements (1,3,5) not in \(A\), so \(B \subset A\) fails.
questions.hint: Check each element of the smaller-looking set against the larger one.
distractor_logic: reverses the containment — B has extra elements (1,3,5) that A lacks
A and B actually share every element of A, so the intersection is A itself, not empty
disjoint means NO shared elements — here they share 2, 4, and 6

topics.name: Sets and Representation
topics.summary: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects — 'well-defined' means there's never any doubt about whether something belongs. Sets are written two ways: roster form lists every element, e.g. \(A=\{1,2,3,4\}\); set-builder form states the defining property, e.g. \(A=\{x : x \in \mathbb{N}, x \le 4\}\). An element's membership uses \(\in\) (belongs to), never \(\subset\) (which relates two sets). Special cases: the empty set \(\emptyset\) has zero elements; a singleton has exactly one; a set is finite if counting its elements terminates, otherwise infinite. Two sets are equal (\(A=B\)) only if they contain exactly the same elements — repeating an element in a listing changes nothing. Two sets are merely equivalent if they simply have the same number of elements, regardless of what those elements are.
key_formulas: \(x \in A\) (membership) vs \(A \subset B\) (containment) — never interchange them
\(A=B\) iff every element of A is in B AND every element of B is in A
Equivalent sets: \(n(A)=n(B)\); Equal sets: identical elements (equal \(\Rightarrow\) equivalent, not the converse)
topics.worked_example: Write \(A=\{x : x \in \mathbb{Z}, x^2=9\}\) in roster form. Solve \(x^2=9\): x = 3 or x = −3, both integers. So \(A=\{-3,3\}\) — a finite set with \(n(A)=2\).
common_mistakes: Writing \(2 \subset A\) for an element instead of \(2 \in A\) (element-vs-subset confusion)
Treating {0} or {∅} as the empty set, when only \(\emptyset\) itself has zero elements
Calling two sets 'equal' just because they have the same size (that's only 'equivalent')
Assuming a repeated element in a listing like \(\{1,1,2\}\) changes the set (it doesn't — it's still {1,2})

topics.name: Subsets and Intervals
topics.summary: \(A \subset B\) means every element of A is also in B — it says nothing about relative sizes, and A can even equal B. A proper subset (\(B \subsetneq A\)) must be strictly smaller: contained but not equal. Two universal facts: every set is a subset of itself (\(A \subset A\)), and the empty set is a subset of every set (\(\emptyset \subset A\)), because there's no element in \(\emptyset\) that could ever violate the condition. Subsets of \(\mathbb{R}\) are often written as intervals: a square bracket includes the endpoint (closed, from \(\le\) or \(\ge\)), a round bracket excludes it (open, from strict \(<\) or \(>\)). So \([a,b]\) includes both ends, \((a,b)\) excludes both, and \([a,b)\) or \((a,b]\) mix the two. Reading interval notation correctly — endpoint by endpoint — is essential for both algebra and Venn-diagram problems later in the syllabus.
key_formulas: \(A \subset A\) always; \(\emptyset \subset A\) for every set A
Bracket rule: \([\) / \(]\) = included (≤, ≥); \((\) / \()\) = excluded (<, >)
A set with n elements has \(2^n\) subsets in total, and \(2^n-1\) proper subsets
topics.worked_example: Is \(B=\{2,4,6\}\) a subset of \(A=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\)? Check each element of B: 2, 4, and 6 are all in A. So \(B \subset A\). Separately, \(\{x \in \mathbb{R}: -3 \le x<4\}\) in interval form is \([-3,4)\) — closed at −3 (≤), open at 4 (strict <).
common_mistakes: Reversing which set is the subset, e.g. writing \(B \subset A\) as \(A \subset B\)
Thinking \(\emptyset\) is a subset of only finite or only some sets, instead of every set without exception
Swapping bracket meaning — treating round brackets as 'included' and square as 'excluded'
Confusing 'subset' (\(\subset\), sizes can tie) with 'proper subset' (\(\subsetneq\), must be strictly smaller)

topics.name: Power Set and Universal Set
topics.summary: The power set \(P(A)\) is the set of ALL possible subsets of A, including the empty set and A itself as members. If \(n(A)=n\), then \(n(P(A))=2^n\), because each of the n elements independently is either 'in' or 'out' of a given subset — 2 choices per element. A useful special case: \(P(\emptyset) = \{\emptyset\}\), a set with exactly one element (the empty set has exactly one subset, itself). Since \(\emptyset \subset A\) always holds, \(\emptyset \in P(A)\) for every set A, without exception. The universal set \(U\) is a separate but related idea: it's simply whatever 'everything relevant to this problem' means in context — not a fixed mathematical object, and not the same thing as a power set. U might be all students in a school for one problem and all integers for another; every other set under discussion is then treated as a subset of that U.
key_formulas: \(P(\emptyset) = \{\emptyset\}\) (has 1 element, is NOT itself empty)
\(\emptyset \in P(A)\) and \(A \in P(A)\) for every set A
topics.worked_example: If \(A=\{x,y,z\}\), then \(n(A)=3\) so \(n(P(A))=2^3=8\). Listed out: \(P(A)=\{\emptyset,\{x\},\{y\},\{z\},\{x,y\},\{y,z\},\{x,z\},\{x,y,z\}\}\) — exactly 8 subsets.
common_mistakes: Computing \(2n\) or \(n^2\) instead of \(2^n\) for the subset count
Forgetting to include \(\emptyset\) or A itself when listing out a power set
Treating \(P(\emptyset)\) as empty, when it actually contains one element
Confusing the universal set U (context-dependent, just 'everything relevant here') with a fixed set like \(\mathbb{R}\)

topics.name: Venn Diagrams
topics.summary: A Venn diagram is the standard picture for set relationships: the universal set U is drawn as a rectangle, and individual sets are circles (or ovals) inside it. The overlap of two circles is \(A \cap B\); the two circles combined is \(A \cup B\); the region inside the rectangle but outside every circle is \((A \cup B)'\) (or \((A \cup B \cup C)'\) for three sets). Circles that don't touch at all represent disjoint sets (\(A \cap B=\emptyset\)). For two sets, the diagram naturally splits into 4 regions: only A, only B, both, and neither. For three sets it splits into 8: three 'only' regions, three 'pairwise-only' regions, one 'all three' region, and 'none'. Reading a labelled diagram is mostly arithmetic once the regions are identified correctly — e.g. \(n(A) = \) 'only A' + 'A & B only' + 'A & C only' + 'all three', since every one of those sub-regions lies inside circle A.
key_formulas: 2-set regions: only A, only B, both, neither (4 total, non-overlapping)
3-set regions: only A, only B, only C, A&B only, B&C only, A&C only, all three (7 total) + none
\(n(A) = \) sum of every region that lies inside circle A
topics.worked_example: A 2-circle diagram shows only-A = 5, only-B = 7, both = 3. Then \(n(A \cup B)=5+7+3=15\) (all three regions together), and if \(n(U)=20\), the 'neither' region is \(20-15=5\).
common_mistakes: Reading the overlap region as \(A \cup B\) instead of \(A \cap B\)
Forgetting the overlap region entirely when adding up regions for the union
Double-counting the 'all three' region when summing a three-set diagram
Leaving out one of the seven regions when computing \(n(A \cup B \cup C)\) from a labelled diagram

topics.name: Operations on Sets
topics.summary: Three core operations combine sets. Union \(A \cup B = \{x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}\) collects everything from either set. Intersection \(A \cap B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}\) keeps only what's shared. Difference \(A-B\) keeps A's elements after removing anything also in B (note \(A-B\) and \(B-A\) are generally different sets). If A and B are disjoint, \(A \cap B = \emptyset\). Several algebraic laws govern these operations: commutative (\(A \cup B = B \cup A\), \(A \cap B = B \cap A\)), associative (regrouping three sets under the same operation doesn't change the result), distributive (\(A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)\), and the mirror version swapping \(\cup\) and \(\cap\)), and idempotent (\(A \cup A = A \cap A = A\)). Multi-set expressions like \(A \cap (B \cup C)\) are always evaluated bracket-first, just like ordinary algebra.
key_formulas: \(A \cup B, \ A \cap B, \ A-B\) (union, intersection, difference)
Commutative: \(A \cup B=B \cup A\); Distributive: \(A \cup (B\cap C)=(A\cup B)\cap(A\cup C)\)
Idempotent: \(A \cup A = A \cap A = A\); Identity: \(A \cup \emptyset=A\), \(A \cap \emptyset=\emptyset\)
common_mistakes: Swapping union and intersection — treating 'or' (union) as 'and' (intersection) or vice versa
Computing \(B-A\) when the question asked for \(A-B\) (difference is not commutative)
Evaluating a compound expression left-to-right instead of bracket-first
Misstating the distributive law by dropping one of the two operations, e.g. writing \(A \cup (B\cap C)=(A\cup B)\cup C\)

topics.name: Complement of a Set
topics.summary: The complement of A (relative to universal set U), written \(A'\), is \(\{x \in U : x \notin A\}\) — everything in U that A leaves out. Two elements can never satisfy 'in A' and 'not in A' simultaneously, so \(A \cap A' = \emptyset\); and together A and \(A'\) cover every element of U, so \(A \cup A' = U\). Complementing twice returns the original set: \((A')' = A\). The complement of U itself is empty (\(U' = \emptyset\)), and the complement of \(\emptyset\) is U. De Morgan's laws connect complements with union and intersection: \((A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'\) ('not (A or B)' becomes 'not A and not B') and \((A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'\) ('not (A and B)' becomes 'not A or not B'). These extend naturally to three sets: \((A \cup B \cup C)' = A' \cap B' \cap C'\), found by complementing the whole union in one step, or by taking the complement of each set and intersecting.
key_formulas: \(A' = \{x \in U : x \notin A\}\); \(A \cup A'=U\); \(A \cap A'=\emptyset\)
De Morgan: \((A \cup B)'=A' \cap B'\) and \((A \cap B)'=A' \cup B'\)
\((A')'=A\); \(U'=\emptyset\); \(\emptyset'=U\)
topics.worked_example: If \(U=\{1,\dots,10\}\) and \(A=\{2,4,6,8,10\}\), then \(A'=\{1,3,5,7,9\}\) (the odd numbers). Checked against De Morgan with \(B=\{1,2,3\}\): \((A\cup B)'\) and \(A' \cap B'\) both work out to the same set.
common_mistakes: Flipping the wrong operation in De Morgan's law, e.g. writing \((A\cup B)'=A'\cup B'\) instead of using \(\cap\)
Believing \(A \cap A'\) could be non-empty, forgetting no element can be both 'in' and 'not in' A
Treating \(U'\) as U itself instead of \(\emptyset\)
Computing the complement of an intersection/union of THREE sets by complementing only one or two of them

topics.name: Practical Problems on Sets
topics.summary: Practical (word) problems use the cardinal number formulas to count survey-style data without drawing every element. For two sets: \(n(A \cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A \cap B)\) — simple addition double-counts the overlap, so it's subtracted once. If A and B are disjoint, this reduces to plain addition. For three sets, the same idea extends via inclusion–exclusion: \(n(A\cup B\cup C)=n(A)+n(B)+n(C)-n(A\cap B)-n(B\cap C)-n(A\cap C)+n(A\cap B\cap C)\) — every pairwise overlap is subtracted once, but the triple overlap (removed three times by that subtraction) must be added back once. The best strategy for a multi-set word problem is to work from the INSIDE OUT: find the triple overlap first (if unknown), then each 'pairwise-only' region (pairwise total minus the triple), then each 'only-one' region, and finally 'none' as \(n(U) - n(A\cup B\cup C)\). Every derived region should stay non-negative — a negative region signals an arithmetic or setup error.
key_formulas: \(n(A \cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A \cap B)\)
\(n(A\cup B\cup C)=n(A)+n(B)+n(C)-n(A\cap B)-n(B\cap C)-n(A\cap C)+n(A\cap B\cap C)\)
Disjoint case: \(n(A \cup B)=n(A)+n(B)\); None \(= n(U) - n(A\cup B \cup C)\)
topics.worked_example: In a class of 50, 30 play cricket, 25 play football, 10 play both. At least one game: \(30+25-10=45\). None: \(50-45=5\).
common_mistakes: Adding n(A) and n(B) directly without subtracting the overlap, double-counting shared elements
For three sets, forgetting to add the triple overlap back after subtracting the three pairwise overlaps
Stopping at the 'at least one' (union) count when the question actually asked for 'none'
Building region values that come out negative and not noticing it as a red flag for a setup error
